- **Secondary bone involvement** by systemic lymphoma (stage IV) is much commoner than primary bone lymphoma.
- **Histology:** **diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in about 80% or more**; others follicular, anaplastic large cell, Hodgkin (rare in bone).
- **Adults, peak 40-60 years** (wide range, can occur in children), **male predominance**.
- **Sites:** **femur (commonest)**, pelvis, humerus, tibia, spine; metadiaphyseal.

### Clinical and radiological features
- Bone pain, swelling, pathological fracture (about 20%), cord compression in spinal disease. **B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) uncommon**; the patient often looks **well relative to the size of the lesion**.
- **Radiographs:** **permeative or moth-eaten lysis** with a wide zone of transition, **little or no periosteal reaction**, sometimes mixed lytic-sclerotic; radiographs can look **nearly normal despite extensive marrow involvement** (cortex permeated by small channels rather than destroyed).
- **MRI:** extensive marrow replacement with a **large circumferential soft-tissue mass** around a relatively intact cortex.
- **Ivory vertebra:** Hodgkin lymphoma (differentials: osteoblastic prostate or breast metastasis, Paget disease).
- **Staging:** **PET-CT** (Lugano staging), bone marrow biopsy, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, LDH.

### Management
- **Biopsy** (core, with fresh tissue for flow cytometry); the diagnosis is made on CD20/CD45 positivity.
- **Chemotherapy: R-CHOP** (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisolone) for DLBCL, often followed by **consolidation radiotherapy** to the involved bone (benefit of adding radiotherapy is debated).
- **Surgery has no role in tumour removal.** Orthopaedic roles: **biopsy**, **fixation of pathological or impending fractures** (intramedullary nailing, cemented arthroplasty), decompression for cord compression when unstable.
- **Prognosis is good**: 5-year survival about 70-90% for localised DLBCL of bone, better than for most other primary bone malignancies.

> Exam pearl: An adult with a permeative lytic lesion, a large soft-tissue mass, minimal periosteal reaction and surprisingly few symptoms suggests primary lymphoma of bone. It is CD45/CD20 positive DLBCL, and it is treated with chemotherapy (R-CHOP) with or without radiotherapy, not resection.

## 4. Multiple myeloma and plasmacytoma
### Epidemiology and pathology
- **Commonest primary malignant tumour arising in bone** (when included among bone tumours); bone involvement in about 80% at diagnosis.
- **Age over 40, median about 65-70 years**; **male predominance**; about **twice as common in people of African ancestry**.
- Clonal proliferation of **plasma cells** secreting a **monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein)**: **IgG commonest (about 50%)**, then **IgA (about 20%)**, light-chain-only (about 20%); IgD and non-secretory rare.
- Precursors: **MGUS** (progression about **1% per year**) and smouldering myeloma.
- **Bone destruction:** myeloma cells increase **RANKL** and reduce OPG, activating **osteoclasts**, and secrete **DKK1** (and sclerostin), which **suppresses osteoblasts**. Hence **purely lytic lesions, normal alkaline phosphatase, and a "cold" bone scan**.
- **Histology:** sheets of plasma cells (eccentric "clock-face" nucleus, perinuclear hof), **CD138 and CD38 positive**, kappa or lambda restricted. Amyloid may be present.

### Clinical features (CRAB)
- **C**alcium raised (hypercalcaemia: confusion, constipation, polyuria).
- **R**enal impairment (light-chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcaemia, amyloid).
- **A**naemia (normocytic; marrow replacement): fatigue.
- **B**one disease: **back pain (commonest presenting symptom)**, vertebral collapse, pathological fractures, cord compression.
- Others: recurrent infections (immunoparesis), hyperviscosity, **amyloidosis** (carpal tunnel syndrome, macroglossia), peripheral neuropathy.

### Diagnostic criteria (IMWG 2014)
- **Clonal bone marrow plasma cells 10% or more, or biopsy-proven bony or extramedullary plasmacytoma**, PLUS **one or more myeloma-defining events**:
  - **CRAB** features attributable to the plasma-cell disorder: calcium over 2.75 mmol/L (11 mg/dL), creatinine over 177 micromol/L (2 mg/dL) or clearance under 40 mL/min, haemoglobin under 10 g/dL (or 2 g/dL below normal), **one or more osteolytic lesions** (on CT, low-dose whole-body CT or PET-CT).
  - **SLiM biomarkers**: **Sixty** percent or more clonal plasma cells; **Light-chain** ratio (involved:uninvolved serum free light chain) 100 or more; **MRI** with more than one focal lesion of 5 mm or more.

### Investigations
- **Bloods:** FBC, **ESR very high**, **rouleaux** on smear, calcium, creatinine, albumin, **beta-2 microglobulin**, LDH, **alkaline phosphatase normal**.
- **Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation** (M band), **serum free light-chain assay**, **urine for Bence Jones protein** (light chains; not detected by dipstick).
- **Bone marrow aspirate and trephine**, with cytogenetics/FISH.
- **Imaging:**
  - **Whole-body low-dose CT** is now preferred over the conventional skeletal survey (IMWG); **PET-CT** and **whole-body MRI** (spine and pelvis; detects marrow infiltration and SLiM focal lesions).
  - **Bone scan is unreliable (false negative)** because there is little osteoblastic activity: in suspected myeloma use radiographs/CT/MRI, not scintigraphy.
- **Radiographic signs:** **"punched-out" lytic lesions without a sclerotic rim**, **"raindrop" (pepper-pot) skull**, diffuse osteopenia, vertebral collapse (**pedicles usually spared early**, as the pedicle has less red marrow; contrast metastases, the "winking owl" sign), expansile lytic lesion in a rib or pelvis. **Sclerotic myeloma** occurs in **POEMS syndrome** (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein, skin changes).

### Staging
| System | Basis |
|---|---|
| **ISS (International Staging System)** | **Stage I:** beta-2 microglobulin under 3.5 mg/L and albumin 3.5 g/dL or more. **Stage III:** beta-2 microglobulin 5.5 mg/L or more. **Stage II:** neither I nor III |
| **R-ISS (Revised ISS)** | Adds **LDH** and **high-risk cytogenetics** (del(17p), t(4;14), t(14;16)) |
| Durie-Salmon | Older system based on Hb, calcium, M-protein level and number of bone lesions |

### Management
- **Systemic therapy (haematology):** triplet or quadruplet regimens, e.g. **bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor), lenalidomide (immunomodulator), dexamethasone (VRd)**, often with the anti-CD38 antibody **daratumumab**; **autologous stem-cell transplantation** in fit patients; newer CAR-T and bispecific antibodies for relapse.
- **Bone-targeted therapy:** **zoledronic acid** (reduces skeletal events and has a modest survival benefit, MRC Myeloma IX) or **denosumab** (useful in renal impairment); calcium and vitamin D; watch for **osteonecrosis of the jaw**.
- **Avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic contrast**; hydrate.
- **Radiotherapy:** pain control, impending fracture, cord compression (myeloma is **very radiosensitive**; low doses, e.g. 8 Gy single fraction or 20 Gy in 5 fractions).
- **Orthopaedic and spinal surgery:**
  - **Biopsy any solitary lytic lesion** before fixation if the diagnosis is not established (a solitary lytic lesion may be myeloma, renal metastasis or primary sarcoma).
  - **Prophylactic fixation of impending fractures** and fixation of pathological fractures: **intramedullary nailing protecting the whole bone**, cemented arthroplasty for the femoral neck, cement augmentation. **Pathological fractures in myeloma have the highest healing rate** of all bone metastatic lesions (about two-thirds heal; Gainor and Buchert).
  - **Vertebral compression fractures:** **kyphoplasty or vertebroplasty** for painful fractures (**CAFE trial**, Berenson 2011: kyphoplasty improved pain and function in cancer-related fractures, mostly myeloma); brace.
  - **Cord compression:** dexamethasone and radiotherapy are first-line (radiosensitive); surgery for spinal instability, bony retropulsion or neurological deterioration despite radiotherapy.

### Solitary plasmacytoma
- **Solitary plasmacytoma of bone:** a single lytic lesion of clonal plasma cells with **no CRAB features** and normal (or under 10% clonal) marrow.
- **Commonest in the spine (vertebral body)**, then pelvis, femur, ribs; younger than myeloma (median about 55).
- **Treatment: radiotherapy about 40-50 Gy** (local control over 85%); surgery for instability or fracture.
- **About 50-70% progress to multiple myeloma within 10 years**: follow with SPEP and free light chains.
- **Extramedullary plasmacytoma** (soft tissue, upper aerodynamic tract) has a lower rate of progression.

> Exam pearl: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with normal ALP and a falsely negative bone scan, because osteoblasts are suppressed. Image with whole-body low-dose CT, PET-CT or MRI. A solitary lytic lesion in a patient over 40 must be biopsied before fixation.

## 5. Metastatic neuroblastoma
- **Commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood**; **most present under 5 years (median about 18 months)**; arises from neural crest cells of the **adrenal medulla** or sympathetic chain.
- **Commonest cause of bone metastases in children under 5**; metastases to **skull and orbit (periorbital bruising, "raccoon eyes", proptosis)**, long-bone metaphyses (lytic, permeative, symmetric lesions), marrow ("Hutchinson" type spread to bone).
- **Clinical:** abdominal mass crossing the midline, limp, bone pain, irritability, fever (mimics osteomyelitis or leukaemia); opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome; **Horner syndrome** (cervical/thoracic).
- **Investigations:** **raised urinary catecholamine metabolites (VMA and HVA)**; **MIBG scintigraphy** (iodine-123 metaiodobenzylguanidine) for primary and metastases; marrow biopsy.
- **Histology:** small round blue cells with **Homer Wright rosettes**, neuropil.
- **Prognosis:** better under 18 months; **MYCN amplification**, unfavourable histology (Shimada) and 11q loss are adverse. **Stage MS (formerly 4S)**: infants under 18 months with limited metastases (skin, liver, marrow) may regress spontaneously.
- **Spinal "dumbbell" tumour** through the neural foramen can cause cord compression and later post-laminectomy or post-radiation **kyphosis or scoliosis**.

## 6. Rhabdomyosarcoma and leukaemia (orthopaedic relevance)
### Rhabdomyosarcoma
- **Commonest soft-tissue sarcoma of childhood**.

| Type | Features |
|---|---|
| **Embryonal** (commonest) | Younger children (under 10), head and neck, genitourinary (**botryoid** variant: grape-like vaginal or bladder mass); better prognosis |
| **Alveolar** | **Adolescents, extremities** and trunk; **t(2;13) PAX3-FOXO1** or t(1;13) PAX7-FOXO1; worse prognosis; can metastasise to bone and marrow (mimics leukaemia) and lymph nodes |
| Pleomorphic | Adults; high grade |

- **Treatment:** multi-agent chemotherapy (**VAC: vincristine, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide**) plus local control by surgery and/or radiotherapy; **regional lymph-node evaluation** (sentinel node biopsy) for extremity tumours.

### Acute leukaemia
- **ALL is the commonest childhood cancer**; up to about a third present with **bone pain, limp or arthralgia** and may be misdiagnosed as **juvenile idiopathic arthritis or osteomyelitis**.
- **Radiographic clues:** **metaphyseal lucent bands ("leukaemic lines")**, diffuse osteopenia, vertebral compression fractures, permeative lesions.
- **Red flags:** night pain, pain out of proportion to joint signs, cytopenias, blasts on smear, raised LDH and uric acid, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy. **Do a peripheral smear before starting steroids for "JIA".**

## 7. Comparison of the main small round cell tumours of bone
| Feature | Ewing sarcoma | Lymphoma of bone | Myeloma | Neuroblastoma metastasis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Age | 5-25 (peak 10-15) | 40-60 (any) | Over 40 (median 65-70) | Under 5 |
| Site | Femur diaphysis, pelvis, ribs | Femur, pelvis, spine | Spine, skull, ribs, pelvis, proximal long bones | Skull, orbit, metaphyses |
| Radiograph | Permeative lysis, onion skin, big soft-tissue mass | Permeative, minimal periosteal reaction, big soft-tissue mass | Punched-out lysis, no sclerotic rim | Symmetric lytic metaphyseal lesions |
| Key test | CD99, EWSR1-FLI1 | CD45, CD20 | M-protein, CD138, marrow | Urine VMA/HVA, MIBG |
| Bone scan | Hot | Hot | **Often cold** | Hot (MIBG better) |
| Mainstay of treatment | Chemo plus surgery and/or RT | Chemo (R-CHOP) plus or minus RT | Systemic therapy, bisphosphonate, RT | Chemo, surgery, RT, immunotherapy |

> Exam pearl: Age sorts the round cell tumours: neuroblastoma under 5, Ewing 5-25, lymphoma in middle age, myeloma after 40-50. Radiosensitive lesions in this group (Ewing, lymphoma, myeloma, plasmacytoma) explain why radiotherapy has a much larger role here than in osteosarcoma or chondrosarcoma.

soft-tissue sarcoma.md:
## 1. Epidemiology and general features
- Soft-tissue sarcomas (STS) are malignant tumours of **mesenchymal origin** (fat, muscle, fibrous tissue, vessels, nerve sheath); **about 1% of adult cancers** but over **70 histological subtypes** (WHO 2020).
- **Benign soft-tissue tumours outnumber sarcomas by about 100:1**; **lipoma** is the commonest soft-tissue tumour.
- **Age:** any; most in adults over 50. In **children the commonest STS is rhabdomyosarcoma**.
- **Commonest STS in adults:** **undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS)** and **liposarcoma** are the two commonest (which is first varies by series; for extremity sarcomas in older adults UPS is often quoted, for all sites liposarcoma).
- **Site:** **extremities about 50-60%** (**lower limb, especially the thigh, is the commonest site**), trunk wall, **retroperitoneum about 15%**, head and neck, viscera.
- **Behaviour:** grow centrifugally and compress surrounding tissue into a **pseudocapsule (reactive zone)** containing **satellite tumour cells**, with **skip lesions** in high-grade tumours. **Shelling out through the pseudocapsule leaves tumour behind**, which is why wide excision is needed.
- **Spread:** **haematogenous**, **lungs commonest (about 80% of metastases)**. Lymph-node metastasis is **uncommon (under 5%) except in specific subtypes** (see below).
- **Predisposing factors:**
  - **Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53)**, **neurofibromatosis type 1** (MPNST), **hereditary retinoblastoma (RB1)**, **familial adenomatous polyposis/Gardner syndrome** (desmoid tumours), Werner syndrome.
  - **Prior radiotherapy** (radiation-associated sarcoma, latency usually over 5-10 years; angiosarcoma, UPS).
  - **Chronic lymphoedema** (**Stewart-Treves syndrome**: lymphangiosarcoma/angiosarcoma after mastectomy and axillary clearance).
  - Chemicals (vinyl chloride: hepatic angiosarcoma), HIV/HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma).

## 2. Clinical evaluation of a soft-tissue mass
- Typical sarcoma: **painless, enlarging mass**; pain occurs in about a third. Patients often attribute it to trauma ("haematoma" that does not resolve).
- **Red-flag features of a soft-tissue lump (suspect sarcoma):**
  - **Size over 5 cm** (golf ball)
  - **Deep to the deep fascia**
  - **Increasing in size**
  - **Painful**
  - **Recurrence after previous excision**
- **Any one** feature warrants referral and imaging; deep or over 5 cm lumps have a high risk (about 10% or more of deep lumps over 5 cm are malignant). Superficial small lumps can still be sarcoma (e.g. epithelioid, myxofibrosarcoma).
- **Examination:** size, depth, consistency, mobility, transillumination, pulsatility, neurovascular status (Tinel sign over a nerve sheath tumour), **regional lymph nodes**, skin changes.

## 3. Investigations
- **Ultrasound:** first-line triage of superficial lumps (UK pathway); sarcoma suspected if **heterogeneous, vascular, deep, or over 5 cm**.
- **MRI with gadolinium: investigation of choice** for local evaluation: size, compartment, depth, relation to **neurovascular bundle and bone**, peritumoural oedema, necrosis; plans biopsy and surgery.
  - **Lipoma** is homogeneous fat signal, suppresses completely on fat-saturated sequences, with only thin septa.
  - **Atypical lipomatous tumour (ALT)**: thick (over 2 mm) or nodular septa, non-fatty areas, large size, deep location.
  - **Myxoid tumours** (myxoid liposarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, myxoma) can look **cyst-like** (high T2) but **enhance** with contrast: never call a deep "cyst" benign without contrast.
- **Plain radiographs:** bone involvement, **calcification** (synovial sarcoma about 30%, phleboliths in haemangioma, myositis ossificans zonation), extraskeletal osteosarcoma.
- **Staging:**
  - **CT chest** for all intermediate- or high-grade sarcomas (lungs are the commonest metastatic site).
  - **Myxoid (round cell) liposarcoma:** metastasises to **extrapulmonary sites** (spine, retroperitoneum, other soft tissue) and may be missed by CT and PET: add **whole-spine MRI or whole-body MRI**.
  - **Lymph-node assessment** (clinical, ultrasound, CT/PET, sentinel node biopsy in selected cases) for node-seeking subtypes.
  - **CT abdomen/pelvis** for myxoid liposarcoma, retroperitoneal tumours and leiomyosarcoma; brain MRI for **alveolar soft part sarcoma** and angiosarcoma.
  - **PET-CT:** useful for high-grade tumours, rhabdomyosarcoma, NF1 (suspected malignant change in a plexiform neurofibroma) and response assessment.

### Biopsy principles (Mankin)
- **Biopsy after all imaging**, at (or after discussion with) **the specialist sarcoma centre that will perform definitive surgery**. **Mankin et al. (1982, repeated 1996)**: biopsies performed in referring hospitals had **significantly more diagnostic errors, complications and changes in treatment (including unnecessary amputation)** than those performed in treating centres.
- **Image-guided core needle biopsy** is the standard (diagnostic accuracy over 90%); open incisional biopsy if core is non-diagnostic. **Fine-needle aspiration is not adequate** for primary diagnosis (no architecture or grade).
- **Rules:**
  - **Longitudinal** incision in the limb (in line with the definitive resection), as small as possible.
  - Through a **single compartment**; avoid intermuscular planes, joints and the **neurovascular bundle**.
  - Meticulous haemostasis; if a drain is used, it exits **in line with and close to the incision**.
  - Biopsy tract is considered contaminated and **excised en bloc** with the tumour.
  - Sample the **enhancing, viable periphery** (avoid necrotic centre); send fresh tissue for **molecular genetics** and cultures where infection is possible.
- **Excisional biopsy** is acceptable only for **small (under 3-5 cm), superficial** lesions where re-excision would be straightforward.

## 4. Grading and staging
### FNCLCC (French) grading system: the standard histological grade
| Parameter | Score |
|---|---|
| **Tumour differentiation** | 1 = closely resembles normal adult mesenchymal tissue; 2 = histological type certain; 3 = embryonal, undifferentiated, or type uncertain |
| **Mitotic count (per 10 high-power fields)** | 1 = 0-9; 2 = 10-19; 3 = 20 or more |
| **Tumour necrosis** | 0 = none; 1 = under 50%; 2 = 50% or more |
| **Total score** | **2-3 = Grade 1**; **4-5 = Grade 2**; **6-8 = Grade 3** |

- **Grade is the most important predictor of distant metastasis** (and overall survival); **margin status is the most important predictor of local recurrence**.

### AJCC 8th edition: trunk and extremity sarcoma
| T stage | Size |
|---|---|
| T1 | 5 cm or less |
| T2 | Over 5 cm up to 10 cm |
| T3 | Over 10 cm up to 15 cm |
| T4 | Over 15 cm |

| Stage | Definition |
|---|---|
| IA | T1, N0, M0, grade 1 (or GX) |
| IB | T2-T4, N0, M0, grade 1 (or GX) |
| II | T1, N0, M0, grade 2-3 |
| IIIA | T2, N0, M0, grade 2-3 |
| IIIB | T3-T4, N0, M0, grade 2-3 |
| IV | **Any N1 or any M1** |

- **Depth (superficial vs deep) was removed from the AJCC 8th edition staging** (it was in the 7th), though it remains prognostic and is still a red flag.
- **Retroperitoneal sarcomas** have a separate AJCC staging; Enneking staging (low/high grade, intra/extracompartmental, metastasis) is still used by orthopaedic oncologists, particularly for musculoskeletal surgical planning.

## 5. Important subtypes (high-yield table)
| Subtype | Typical patient and site | Key pathology/genetics | Behaviour and exam points |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Atypical lipomatous tumour / well-differentiated liposarcoma** | Older adults; **ALT in limbs**, WDL in retroperitoneum | **MDM2 and CDK4 amplification (12q13-15 ring/giant marker chromosomes)**; MDM2 FISH distinguishes from lipoma | **Does not metastasise**; local recurrence; **marginal excision acceptable in limbs**; risk of **dedifferentiation** (higher in retroperitoneum) |
| **Myxoid liposarcoma** (including round-cell) | Young-middle-aged adults (30-50), **thigh** | **t(12;16) FUS-DDIT3** (rarely t(12;22) EWSR1-DDIT3); **"chicken-wire" capillaries**, lipoblasts | **Very radiosensitive** and chemosensitive (trabectedin); **extrapulmonary metastases** (spine, retroperitoneum, soft tissues); round-cell over 5% = higher grade |
| Pleomorphic and dedifferentiated liposarcoma | Older adults | Pleomorphic lipoblasts; dedifferentiated keeps MDM2 amplification | High grade |
| **Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS)** | **Elderly (over 50-60), thigh**, deep | Diagnosis of exclusion; formerly "malignant fibrous histiocytoma" | High grade; lung metastases; also arises in bone (infarct, Paget, radiation) |
| **Myxofibrosarcoma** | Elderly, **superficial**, limbs | Myxoid stroma, curvilinear vessels | **Infiltrative "tail sign" along fascia on MRI**; **very high local recurrence**; needs wide margins |
| **Synovial sarcoma** | **Adolescents and young adults (15-40)**, **around the knee (popliteal fossa)**, foot and ankle; **rarely intra-articular** despite the name | **t(X;18)(p11;q11) SS18-SSX1/SSX2**; **TLE1** and **SS18-SSX fusion-specific antibody** positive; biphasic or monophasic | Often **slow-growing and painful**, may be small and mistaken for benign; **calcification in about 30%** on radiographs; **chemosensitive (ifosfamide)**; lymph-node metastases; late metastases |
| **Epithelioid sarcoma** | **Young adults, hand, wrist and forearm (commonest STS of the hand in many series)** | **Loss of INI1 (SMARCB1)**; keratin and EMA positive | Ulcerating nodules mistaken for **granuloma, infection or rheumatoid nodule**; spreads along fascia and tendons; **lymph-node metastases**; tazemetostat (EZH2 inhibitor) |
| **Clear cell sarcoma ("melanoma of soft parts")** | Young adults, **foot and ankle tendons and aponeuroses** | **t(12;22) EWSR1-ATF1**; **S100, HMB-45, Melan-A positive** (melanocytic markers) | Lymph-node metastases; poor prognosis; distinguished from melanoma by the fusion |
| **Alveolar soft part sarcoma** | Adolescents and young adults, thigh/buttock | **t(X;17) ASPSCR1-TFE3**; TFE3 nuclear | Highly vascular; **metastases to lung and brain** early; responds to immune checkpoint inhibitors |
| **Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)** | About half in **NF1** (lifetime risk about 8-13%), sciatic nerve, brachial plexus | S100 patchy or lost, loss of H3K27me3 | Suspect when a **plexiform neurofibroma becomes painful or grows rapidly, or a new neurological deficit appears**; FDG-PET (high SUV) guides biopsy; poor prognosis |
| **Leiomyosarcoma** | Middle-aged and elderly; **retroperitoneum, IVC**, uterus, limbs (vascular origin) | Desmin, SMA, h-caldesmon | Haematogenous spread |
| **Angiosarcoma** | Elderly scalp, post-radiation breast, **Stewart-Treves** (lymphoedematous arm) | CD31, ERG, CD34 | Very aggressive, multifocal |
| **Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP)** | Young-middle-aged adults, trunk, superficial | **COL1A1-PDGFB**, CD34 positive | Locally aggressive, rarely metastasises; wide excision or **Mohs**; **imatinib** for unresectable |
| **Rhabdomyosarcoma** | Children; alveolar type in adolescent extremities | Desmin, myogenin; PAX3/7-FOXO1 | VAC chemotherapy; lymph nodes |
| **Extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma** | Adults, thigh | NR4A3 rearrangement (EWSR1-NR4A3) | Slow but metastasises |

### Lymph-node-seeking sarcomas (classic list, mnemonic "SCARE")
- **S**ynovial sarcoma, **C**lear cell sarcoma, **A**ngiosarcoma, **R**habdomyosarcoma, **E**pithelioid sarcoma (alveolar soft part sarcoma also).

> Exam pearl: Lymph node spread is rare in sarcoma except SCARE (synovial, clear cell, angiosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, epithelioid). Myxoid liposarcoma spreads to extrapulmonary sites, so stage with whole-spine or whole-body MRI. Grade predicts metastasis; margin predicts local recurrence.

## 6. Intermediate (locally aggressive) tumours: desmoid fibromatosis
- **Desmoid-type (aggressive) fibromatosis:** clonal myofibroblastic proliferation; **locally infiltrative, never metastasises**, but recurs often and can cause morbidity.
- **Genetics:** sporadic tumours have **CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations** (S45F mutation associated with higher recurrence); **APC germline mutation** in **familial adenomatous polyposis/Gardner syndrome** (intra-abdominal, mesenteric desmoids). **Nuclear beta-catenin** on immunohistochemistry.
- Sites: shoulder girdle, chest wall, thigh, abdominal wall (often **postpartum**; oestrogen influence), mesentery.
- **Natural history is unpredictable**: a substantial proportion stabilise or **regress spontaneously**.
- **Management (Desmoid Tumor Working Group global consensus 2020):**
  1. **Active surveillance first-line** for most asymptomatic or non-threatening tumours, with MRI after 1-2 months and then every 3-6 months.
  2. Treat only if **persistent progression** or symptoms, or threat to vital structures.
  3. **Systemic therapy is preferred over surgery** for progressive disease: **nirogacestat** (gamma-secretase inhibitor; **DeFi trial**, NEJM 2023, improved progression-free survival), **sorafenib** (Gounder et al., NEJM 2018), low-dose methotrexate-vinblastine, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, NSAIDs/hormonal agents (weak evidence).
  4. **Surgery** (aiming for negative margins without major functional loss) for selected progressive limb or abdominal-wall tumours; **positive margins are often watched** rather than re-excised. Radiotherapy, cryoablation are alternatives.

## 7. Management of soft-tissue sarcoma
### Surgery: wide local excision is the mainstay
- **Margins (Enneking):**

| Margin | Plane | Local recurrence (without radiotherapy) |
|---|---|---|
| **Intralesional** | Through the tumour | Almost certain |
| **Marginal** | Through the **reactive zone/pseudocapsule** | High for high-grade tumours (satellite cells) |
| **Wide** | Through normal tissue with a **cuff of normal tissue** around the reactive zone | Acceptable, especially combined with radiotherapy |
| **Radical** | **Entire compartment** removed (or amputation proximal to the compartment) | Lowest; rarely needed now |

- In practice, a **wide margin of about 1-2 cm of normal tissue, or an intact fascial barrier** (fascia, periosteum, epineurium, vessel adventitia act as barriers), is aimed for. **R0** = microscopically negative, **R1** = microscopic tumour at margin, **R2** = macroscopic tumour left.
- **Limb salvage is possible in over 90% of extremity sarcomas**. **Rosenberg et al. (NCI, 1982):** **limb-sparing surgery plus radiotherapy gave the same overall survival as amputation** (higher local recurrence, but no survival difference). This established limb salvage.
- **Amputation** indications: tumour encasing major neurovascular structures where reconstruction is impossible or would leave a useless limb, extensive contamination (failed previous surgery, fungating tumour), recurrence after maximum radiotherapy, patient choice.
- Neurovascular involvement: **vascular resection and reconstruction** (graft) is possible; **epineurial dissection** if the nerve is abutted, nerve resection if encased (sciatic resection may still give a functional limb).
- Soft-tissue reconstruction: local or **free flaps** (especially after preoperative radiotherapy to reduce wound complications).

### Unplanned excision ("whoops procedure")
- Excision of a mass without preoperative imaging and assumed to be benign, later found to be a sarcoma; usually **intralesional or marginal**.
- **Residual tumour is found in about 40-50% of re-excision specimens**.
- Management: refer to a sarcoma centre, **MRI (and staging)**, then **re-excision of the entire tumour bed and scar with wide margins**, usually with radiotherapy. Prognosis after appropriate re-excision approaches that of planned surgery, but morbidity (larger resections, flaps) is higher.

### Radiotherapy
- **Indications:** most **intermediate- and high-grade, deep or over 5 cm** tumours, and **close or positive margins**. Low-grade, small, superficial tumours excised with wide margins may need surgery alone.
- **Yang et al. (NCI, 1998)** randomised trial: adjuvant external-beam radiotherapy after limb-sparing surgery **reduced local recurrence but did not change overall survival**.
- **Preoperative versus postoperative radiotherapy: O'Sullivan et al. (NCIC SR2, Lancet 2002):**

| Feature | **Preoperative RT (50 Gy)** | **Postoperative RT (60-66 Gy)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Major wound complications** | **Higher (about 35%)** | Lower (about 17%) |
| **Late toxicity** (fibrosis, joint stiffness, oedema) | **Lower** (Davis 2005) | **Higher** |
| Dose and field | Lower dose, smaller field | Higher dose, larger field (whole surgical bed) |
| Local control and survival | **Equivalent** | Equivalent |
| Other | Tumour may shrink or become better defined; thigh wounds worst | Full pathology available first |

  - **Current practice favours preoperative radiotherapy** for most extremity STS, because **late toxicity is permanent whereas wound complications are temporary and treatable** (plan plastic surgical closure). Wound complications are commonest in the **lower limb, especially the thigh**.
  - Preoperative radiotherapy is particularly useful for **myxoid liposarcoma** (very radiosensitive, marked shrinkage).
- **Retroperitoneal sarcoma:** the **STRASS trial (EORTC 62092)** showed **no overall benefit of preoperative radiotherapy** on abdominal recurrence-free survival (a possible benefit in liposarcoma subgroups is debated); surgery is the main treatment (en bloc resection with adjacent organs where needed).
- **Brachytherapy** and **intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT)** reduce dose to normal tissue.

### Chemotherapy
- **Standard drugs: doxorubicin with or without ifosfamide**. Newer: trabectedin (myxoid/round cell liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma), eribulin (liposarcoma), gemcitabine-docetaxel, pazopanib (non-adipocytic sarcomas), **imatinib (GIST, DFSP)**, immune checkpoint inhibitors (UPS, alveolar soft part sarcoma).
- **Adjuvant chemotherapy for adult STS is controversial**: the **EORTC 62931** trial showed **no benefit** of adjuvant doxorubicin-ifosfamide; meta-analyses (e.g. Sarcoma Meta-analysis Collaboration, Pervaiz 2008) show a **small benefit in local and distant recurrence with a marginal overall survival benefit**. Generally offered for **high-risk (large, high-grade, deep) tumours of chemosensitive subtypes**, often as neoadjuvant therapy (ISG-STS 1001 supports histology-tailored or standard anthracycline-ifosfamide neoadjuvant regimens).
- **Chemotherapy is a standard component** for **rhabdomyosarcoma, extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma** and is commonly used in **synovial sarcoma** and **myxoid liposarcoma** (chemosensitive).
- **Isolated limb perfusion** (hyperthermic, **melphalan plus TNF-alpha**) for locally advanced, otherwise unresectable extremity sarcomas to avoid amputation.

### Metastatic disease
- **Pulmonary metastasectomy** for limited, resectable lung metastases with a long disease-free interval (about 20-30% long-term survival in selected patients).
- Palliative chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted agents.

### Follow-up
- Local recurrence: clinical examination and **MRI** (or ultrasound) of the primary site; distant: **CT chest** (or chest radiograph); every 3-4 months for 2-3 years for high-grade tumours, then 6-monthly to 5 years, then annually (most recurrences occur within 2-3 years; some subtypes recur late, e.g. synovial sarcoma, ALT).

## 8. Prognosis
- **Overall 5-year survival about 60-65%** for extremity STS (higher for low-grade, under 50% for large high-grade tumours).
- **Predictors of distant metastasis and death:** **high grade**, **large size (over 5 cm, especially over 10 cm)**, **deep location**, older age, certain subtypes (MPNST, angiosarcoma, pleomorphic liposarcoma, UPS), **local recurrence** (marker of aggressive biology).
- **Predictors of local recurrence:** **positive margins (the most important)**, high grade, no radiotherapy, myxofibrosarcoma/infiltrative types, previous recurrence.
- Nomograms (e.g. **Sarculator**, MSKCC) estimate individual risk.

## 9. Differential diagnosis of soft-tissue masses (distractors)
| Lesion | Clues |
|---|---|
| **Lipoma** | Superficial, soft, homogeneous fat on MRI, suppresses on fat-saturation; intramuscular lipoma infiltrates muscle but is still benign |
| **Haematoma** | History of trauma or anticoagulation, should resolve; **a "haematoma" that does not resolve must be imaged with contrast MRI** (haemorrhagic sarcoma) |
| **Myositis ossificans** | After trauma; **zonal pattern: mature peripheral ossification with an immature centre** (opposite of osteosarcoma); early biopsy may mislead (pseudosarcomatous); calcification appears at 3-4 weeks |
| **Nodular fasciitis** | Rapidly growing (weeks) superficial nodule in young adults, forearm; **USP6 rearrangement**; self-limiting |
| **Schwannoma / neurofibroma** | Eccentric (schwannoma) or fusiform central (neurofibroma) along a nerve; **"split-fat", "target" and "fascicular" signs** on MRI; positive Tinel |
| **Haemangioma / vascular malformation** | Phleboliths, varies with position, serpiginous flow voids |
| **Intramuscular myxoma** | Homogeneous, very high T2, thin peripheral fat rim; with fibrous dysplasia in **Mazabraud syndrome** |
| **Ganglion, Baker cyst** | Thin-walled, peripheral enhancement only, communication with joint |
| **Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)** | Low signal on T2 and **blooming** on gradient echo (haemosiderin); CSF1 overexpression; pexidartinib |
| Abscess, tuberculous cold abscess | Systemic features, rim enhancement, fluid on aspiration |

> Exam pearl: A soft-tissue lump that is over 5 cm, deep to fascia, enlarging, painful or recurrent needs contrast MRI and then a core needle biopsy at the sarcoma centre that will do the surgery, never an excision. Treatment is wide excision with radiotherapy (preoperative preferred: more wound complications but less permanent late toxicity, per O'Sullivan NCIC SR2); limb salvage equals amputation for survival (Rosenberg 1982).

metastatic bone disease.md:
## 1. Epidemiology
- **Metastasis is the commonest malignant lesion of bone** (far commoner than primary bone sarcoma); in a patient **over 40 with a destructive bone lesion, metastasis (or myeloma) is the most likely diagnosis**.
- **Bone is the third commonest site of metastasis** (after lung and liver).
- **Primary tumours that commonly metastasise to bone: breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid**; **breast, prostate and lung account for about 80%** of skeletal metastases.
  - Breast and prostate: bone metastases in up to **70%** of advanced disease.
  - **Commonest primary in women: breast**; **in men: prostate** (lung close behind).
- **Commonest site of bone metastasis: spine** (**thoracic about 70%**, lumbar about 20%, cervical about 10%), then **pelvis, ribs, proximal femur** (the **commonest long bone**), skull and **proximal humerus**. Metastases are commonest in **red-marrow-rich axial and proximal appendicular bones**.
- **Acrometastases** (distal to elbow and knee: hand and foot) are rare; the **commonest primary is lung**.
- **Children:** **neuroblastoma** (commonest under 5), Wilms tumour (rare; clear cell sarcoma of kidney is the bone-seeking renal tumour), rhabdomyosarcoma, retinoblastoma.

## 2. Pathophysiology
- **Routes:** haematogenous (main), via **Batson's valveless vertebral venous plexus** (explains spread of **prostate and breast** cancer to the spine and pelvis when intra-abdominal or intrathoracic pressure rises), direct extension (rare).
- **"Seed and soil" hypothesis (Paget):** marrow provides a favourable microenvironment (growth factors, adhesion molecules, chemokines such as CXCL12/CXCR4).
- **The vicious cycle of osteolysis:** tumour cells secrete **PTHrP** (and IL-6, IL-11), which stimulates osteoblasts to express **RANKL** (and reduces OPG); RANKL activates **osteoclasts**; bone resorption releases **TGF-beta, IGF and calcium** from the matrix, which stimulate further tumour growth. Basis for **bisphosphonates and denosumab** (anti-RANKL antibody).
- **Osteoblastic metastases (prostate):** tumour cells secrete **endothelin-1**, Wnt proteins and BMPs, stimulating osteoblasts; the new bone is woven and mechanically weak.
- A lesion must destroy about **30-50% of the bone mineral** before it is visible on radiographs.

### Radiological pattern by primary
| Pattern | Primaries |
|---|---|
| **Purely lytic** | **Kidney (renal cell)**, **thyroid**, lung (non-small cell, most), melanoma, GI tract, adrenal, myeloma |
| **Osteoblastic (sclerotic)** | **Prostate** (classic), carcinoid, small cell lung cancer, medulloblastoma, bladder (occasionally), Hodgkin lymphoma, treated breast cancer |
| **Mixed** | **Breast**, lung, cervix, ovary, testicular |
| **Expansile, "blow-out" lytic** | Renal and thyroid |

- **Renal cell and thyroid metastases are hypervascular**: **preoperative embolisation** reduces blood loss (surgery within about 24-72 hours of embolisation); do not do an unplanned open biopsy or curettage without being ready for major bleeding.

## 3. Clinical features
- **Pain**: the commonest symptom; initially **night and rest pain** (biological), later **mechanical/functional pain on weight bearing** (impending fracture).
- **Pathological fracture**: first presentation in some patients.
- **Hypercalcaemia**: the **commonest metabolic complication** (up to 10-30% of patients with advanced cancer; breast, lung, myeloma; renal through PTHrP): thirst, polyuria, confusion, constipation, nausea, arrhythmias. Treat with **IV fluids, IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid)**, **denosumab** if refractory or renal impairment, calcitonin for rapid short-term effect, steroids in lymphoma/myeloma.
- **Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC)**: back pain (often thoracic, band-like, worse lying down or with straining) precedes neurological deficit; weakness, sensory level, sphincter disturbance late.
- Marrow failure (anaemia), constitutional symptoms.
- **Skeletal-related events (SREs)**: pathological fracture, spinal cord compression, need for radiotherapy or surgery to bone, hypercalcaemia.

## 4. Evaluation of a destructive bone lesion in a patient over 40
### Rougraff diagnostic strategy (Rougraff et al., JBJS 1993): patient with a skeletal metastasis of unknown origin
1. **History** (smoking, weight loss, previous cancer, haematuria, breast lump) and **examination** (breast, prostate, thyroid, abdomen, lymph nodes, skin).
2. **Laboratory:** FBC, ESR, **calcium**, **alkaline phosphatase**, renal and liver function, **serum and urine protein electrophoresis/free light chains (myeloma)**, **PSA** (men), thyroid function and others as indicated. Tumour markers (CEA, CA 15-3, CA-125) are of limited value.
3. **Plain radiographs** of the affected bone (whole bone) and **chest radiograph**.
4. **CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis**.
5. **Whole-body bone imaging: technetium-99m bone scan** (or PET-CT) to find other lesions and the most accessible site for biopsy.
6. **Biopsy** of the most accessible lesion (core needle, image-guided).
- This approach **identified the primary in about 85%** of cases. **Lung (non-small cell) carcinoma was the commonest unknown primary**, followed by **kidney**. In about 10-15% no primary is found ("carcinoma of unknown primary").

> Exam pearl: Never fix a solitary destructive bone lesion until it is proven to be a metastasis. A "solitary metastasis" may be a primary bone sarcoma (needs wide resection, and intramedullary nailing would contaminate the whole bone), myeloma or renal carcinoma (needs embolisation). Biopsy first, following sarcoma biopsy principles; even with a known primary cancer, a first and solitary bone lesion should be biopsied.

### Imaging details
- **Bone scintigraphy (Tc-99m MDP)**: sensitive whole-skeleton survey; **false negatives in purely lytic lesions** (**myeloma**, some **renal and thyroid** metastases, aggressive lytic lesions) and LCH; "**superscan**" (diffuse uptake with absent renal activity) in widespread prostate/breast metastases.
- **PET-CT**: FDG-avid lytic metastases; **PSMA PET-CT** for prostate cancer staging.
- **MRI**: **the most sensitive for marrow and spinal disease**, epidural extension and cord compression; whole-spine MRI for suspected MSCC.
- **CT**: cortical destruction, fracture risk, surgical planning; CT-guided biopsy.

### Spinal clues
- **Vertebral body is involved first**; the **pedicle is destroyed on the AP radiograph ("winking owl" sign)**, because the body and posterior elements are involved together. Myeloma often spares the pedicle early.
- **Disc space is preserved** (tumours rarely cross the disc), in contrast to **pyogenic infection**, which destroys the disc and both endplates; **TB** may spare the disc early and spread subligamentously.
- **Malignant versus osteoporotic vertebral collapse on MRI:**

| Feature | Malignant | Osteoporotic |
|---|---|---|
| Marrow signal | Diffuse T1 low signal replacing the **whole body**, often **multiple non-contiguous levels** | Band-like oedema, **preserved normal fatty marrow** in part of the body |
| Posterior cortex | **Convex bulge** | Retropulsed bony fragment, angular |
| Pedicle / posterior elements | **Involved** | Spared |
| Epidural/paravertebral mass | Present | Absent or thin |
| Other | Diffusion restriction, enhancement | **Fluid sign**, intravertebral vacuum cleft |

## 5. Predicting pathological fracture
### Mirels scoring system (Mirels 1989), long bones
| Variable | 1 point | 2 points | 3 points |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Site** | Upper limb | Lower limb | **Peritrochanteric** |
| **Pain** | Mild | Moderate | **Functional (mechanical)** |
| **Lesion type** | Blastic | Mixed | **Lytic** |
| **Size (fraction of bone diameter on radiograph)** | Under one-third | One-third to two-thirds | **Over two-thirds** |

| Total score | Fracture risk | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **7 or less** | About 4% (low) | **Radiotherapy and observation** |
| **8** | About 15% | **Clinical judgement** |
| **9 or more** | **About 33% or more** | **Prophylactic fixation** |

- Mirels score has **high sensitivity but poor specificity** (many patients scoring 9 would not fracture) and is less reliable for the femur at the margins of the scale; **functional pain is the most important clinical variable**.
- **Other criteria for prophylactic fixation of the femur:**
  - **Harrington's criteria:** **cortical destruction of 50% or more**, **lesion of 2.5 cm or more in the proximal femur**, **pathological avulsion of the lesser trochanter**, and **persistent pain on weight bearing despite radiotherapy**.
  - **Axial cortical involvement over 30 mm** (or circumferential involvement over 50%) on radiographs: the predictor validated in the **Dutch Femoral Metastases study (Van der Linden et al., 2004)**; lesions below this can be treated with radiotherapy alone.
  - **CT-based structural rigidity analysis (CTRA)** and **finite element models** are more accurate but not yet widely available.
- **Expected survival** guides the decision: **orthopaedic surgery is generally considered when expected survival is more than about 6 weeks** (long bones) and **3 months** (spine) in classic teaching; tools such as **PATHFx**, **SPRING** and **Katagiri** scores estimate survival.
- **Healing of pathological fractures (Gainor and Buchert 1983):** **myeloma highest (about 65-70%)**, **renal about 45%**, **breast about 35-40%**, **lung essentially 0%**. Healing depends on survival over 6 months; radiotherapy does not prevent healing but chemotherapy and poor nutrition reduce it. **Implants must therefore be designed to last without bone healing.**

## 6. Principles of surgical management (long bones)
- **Aims:** pain relief, **immediate weight bearing and function**, nursing care, and a construct that **outlasts the patient** (single operation).
- **Multidisciplinary discussion** (oncologist, radiotherapist, orthopaedic oncologist; BOA guidance on metastatic bone disease recommends this for all impending and actual fractures), optimise calcium, haemoglobin, nutrition; **embolise hypervascular lesions** (renal, thyroid, some myeloma).
- **Image the whole bone** (and the other femur) before fixation to detect additional lesions that must be protected.
- **Principles of fixation:**
  1. **Protect the whole bone**: e.g. **long cephalomedullary (reconstruction) nail** for the femur so the femoral neck and entire shaft are protected.
  2. Use **load-bearing or load-sharing** constructs that allow **immediate full weight bearing**.
  3. **Curettage of the lesion and cement augmentation (PMMA)** to fill defects and improve screw purchase (with plates or nails).
  4. **Replace rather than fix** where periarticular bone is destroyed: fractures of the **femoral head and neck do not heal** reliably: use **cemented (long-stem) hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty**, not internal fixation.
  5. **Endoprosthetic (tumour/megaprosthesis) replacement** for extensive metaphyseal or periarticular destruction, failed fixation, or **solitary renal/thyroid metastasis treated for cure**.
- **Postoperative radiotherapy** to the **whole operative field** (entire implant length), usually started **about 2 weeks after surgery** once the wound is healing: **Townsend et al. (1994)** showed **fewer second procedures and better function** with postoperative radiotherapy.
- **Cardiopulmonary complications:** **fat and tumour embolism** with intramedullary reaming and **cemented long stems** (bone cement implantation syndrome): vent the canal, lavage, careful cementing, communicate with anaesthesia.

### Choice of procedure by site
| Site | Preferred treatment |
|---|---|
| **Femoral head/neck** | **Cemented hemiarthroplasty or THA** (long stem if more distal lesions); acetabulum assessed |
| **Intertrochanteric / subtrochanteric** | **Long cephalomedullary nail** (plus cement); **proximal femoral replacement** if extensive destruction or failed fixation |
| **Femoral shaft** | **Locked intramedullary nail** (protect the neck with a reconstruction nail) |
| **Distal femur** | Locking plate plus cement, retrograde nail, or **distal femoral replacement** |
| **Proximal humerus** | Intramedullary nail, plate plus cement, or **proximal humeral endoprosthesis/hemiarthroplasty** |
| **Humeral shaft** | **Locked intramedullary nail** (or plate plus cement) |
| **Tibia** | Intramedullary nail; distal lesions plate plus cement |
| **Pelvis (non-weight-bearing ilium, pubic rami)** | Radiotherapy, non-operative |

### Periacetabular metastases: Harrington classification
| Class | Defect | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Lateral cortices, superior and medial walls **intact** | **Conventional cemented THA** |
| **II** | **Medial wall deficient** | THA with a **protrusio cage/ring or mesh** to transfer load to the rim |
| **III** | **Lateral cortex and superior dome (roof) deficient** | **Harrington procedure:** **Steinmann pins (or screws) driven from the iliac crest into the acetabular region**, reinforced with **cement**, plus cage and cemented cup |
| **IV** | **Solitary lesion treated for cure** (or pelvic discontinuity) | **En bloc resection** and reconstruction |

- Newer minimally invasive options: **percutaneous acetabuloplasty** (cementoplasty), ablation with screw fixation and cement.

## 7. Metastatic spine disease
### Assessment framework: NOMS (Memorial Sloan Kettering)
- **N - Neurological:** degree of **epidural spinal cord compression (ESCC, Bilsky grade)** and myelopathy/radiculopathy.
- **O - Oncological:** **radiosensitivity** of the tumour.
- **M - Mechanical:** instability (**SINS**).
- **S - Systemic:** extent of disease, comorbidity, ability to tolerate surgery, expected survival.

### Bilsky (ESCC) grading on axial T2 MRI
| Grade | Description |
|---|---|
| 0 | Bone-only disease |
| 1a | Epidural impingement **without deformation of the thecal sac** |
| 1b | Thecal sac deformed, **no spinal cord abutment** |
| 1c | Thecal sac deformed, **spinal cord abutted but not compressed** |
| **2** | **Cord compression, CSF still visible** around the cord |
| **3** | **Cord compression, no CSF visible** |

- **Grades 0-1 = low grade**: radiotherapy (or SBRT); **grades 2-3 = high grade**: decompression is considered for radioresistant tumours.

### Radiosensitivity
| Radiosensitive | Radioresistant (to conventional external-beam radiotherapy) |
|---|---|
| **Lymphoma, myeloma/plasmacytoma, seminoma**, small cell lung, **breast**, **prostate** (most), Ewing | **Renal cell, thyroid, melanoma, sarcoma**, non-small cell lung, colon, hepatocellular |

- **Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT)** delivers high doses accurately and overcomes radioresistance; "**separation surgery**" (posterolateral decompression creating a 2-3 mm gap between tumour and cord, plus stabilisation) followed by SBRT is the MSKCC approach for high-grade ESCC of radioresistant tumours.

### Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS; Spine Oncology Study Group, 2010)
| Component | Scores |
|---|---|
| **Location** | **Junctional** (occiput-C2, C7-T2, T11-L1, L5-S1) **3**; mobile (C3-C6, L2-L4) 2; semi-rigid (T3-T10) 1; rigid (S2-S5) 0 |
| **Pain** | **Mechanical pain 3**; occasional non-mechanical pain 1; pain-free 0 |
| **Bone lesion** | Lytic 2; mixed 1; blastic 0 |
| **Radiographic alignment** | **Subluxation/translation 4**; de novo deformity (kyphosis/scoliosis) 2; normal 0 |
| **Vertebral body collapse** | Over 50% collapse 3; under 50% collapse 2; no collapse with over 50% body involved 1; none of these 0 |
| **Posterolateral involvement** (facet, pedicle, costovertebral joint) | Bilateral 3; unilateral 1; none 0 |

- **Total 0-6 = stable**; **7-12 = indeterminate (potentially unstable)**; **13-18 = unstable**. **Surgical consultation is recommended for a score of 7 or more.**

### Survival scores used to choose surgery
| Score | Components | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **Revised Tokuhashi (0-15)** | General condition (Karnofsky), extraspinal bone metastases, vertebral metastases, visceral metastases, primary site, neurological deficit | **0-8: under 6 months** (conservative/palliative); **9-11: 6 months or more** (palliative surgery); **12-15: 1 year or more** (excisional surgery) |
| **Tomita (2-10)** | Primary tumour growth rate (slow 1, moderate 2, rapid 4), visceral metastases (none 0, treatable 2, untreatable 4), bone metastases (solitary 1, multiple 2) | **2-3: wide or marginal excision (en bloc, long-term control)**; **4-5: marginal or intralesional excision**; **6-7: palliative surgery**; **8-10: supportive care** |

### Treatment of metastatic spinal cord compression
- **Immediate:** **dexamethasone** (e.g. 16 mg/day; higher bolus doses debated), analgesia, flat bed rest and spinal precautions if instability is suspected; **urgent whole-spine MRI (UK NICE: within 24 hours)**; spinal oncology and clinical oncology referral.
- **Patchell et al. (Lancet 2005) randomised trial:** **direct decompressive surgery (circumferential decompression and stabilisation) plus radiotherapy** versus **radiotherapy alone** for MSCC from a solid tumour:
  - **84% vs 57% able to walk after treatment**; **non-ambulant patients regained walking in 62% vs 19%**; walking retained longer (median 122 vs 13 days); less steroid and opioid use; trial stopped early for benefit.
  - **Inclusion:** single area of compression, **expected survival 3 months or more**, **paraplegia for less than 48 hours**, **not radiosensitive tumours** (lymphoma, myeloma, leukaemia, germ-cell excluded).
- **Radiotherapy alone:** radiosensitive tumours, poor surgical candidates, multilevel disease, long-standing complete paraplegia (over 48 hours), short life expectancy.
- **Surgical options:** posterior decompression and **instrumented stabilisation** (laminectomy alone is contraindicated when the anterior column is involved, as it worsens instability), separation surgery, corpectomy and reconstruction, **en bloc spondylectomy (Tomita)** for solitary renal or thyroid metastasis with good prognosis; **minimally invasive percutaneous screw fixation**.
- **Vertebral augmentation (vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty)** for painful pathological compression fractures without significant epidural disease or instability: **CAFE trial (Berenson et al., Lancet Oncology 2011)**: **balloon kyphoplasty gave rapid and sustained improvement in pain and function** compared with non-surgical care. Cement leakage is the commonest complication.

## 8. Non-surgical treatment
### Radiotherapy
- Pain relief in about **60-70%** of patients, often within 2-4 weeks.
- **Single fraction 8 Gy gives the same pain relief as multiple fractions** (e.g. 30 Gy in 10, 20 Gy in 5), confirmed by **RTOG 9714** and the **Dutch Bone Metastasis Study**; **retreatment rate is higher after single fraction (about 18-20% vs 8-10%)**. Single fraction is preferred for uncomplicated painful metastases and poor prognosis.
- **Stereotactic (SBRT)** for oligometastases, radioresistant tumours and re-irradiation; risk of **vertebral compression fracture** after SBRT.
- **Radiopharmaceuticals:** **radium-223** (alpha emitter; **ALSYMPCA trial**: improved overall survival in castration-resistant prostate cancer with bone metastases), strontium-89 and samarium-153 (palliation, marrow suppression).

### Bone-targeted agents
- **Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid):** inhibit osteoclasts (**farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase** in the mevalonate pathway); **reduce skeletal-related events** in breast, prostate, lung cancer and myeloma; treat hypercalcaemia.
- **Denosumab (monoclonal antibody against RANKL):** **superior to zoledronic acid in delaying the first SRE** in breast (Stopeck et al., 2010) and prostate cancer (Fizazi et al., 2011); no renal dose adjustment but risk of **hypocalcaemia** (give calcium and vitamin D); rebound bone loss on stopping.
- **Complications:** **osteonecrosis of the jaw** (dental assessment before starting), **atypical femoral fractures** (lateral cortical beaking: watch for thigh pain), acute-phase reaction, renal toxicity (zoledronic acid).
- **Systemic oncological therapy** (hormonal therapy for breast and prostate, targeted agents, immunotherapy) controls disease and improves healing.
- **Analgesia** (WHO ladder), physiotherapy, orthoses, palliative care.

## 9. Special situations
- **Solitary renal cell carcinoma metastasis:** **wide (en bloc) excision** may **improve survival** (especially metachronous solitary lesions after nephrectomy with a long disease-free interval); **embolise preoperatively**; renal metastases respond poorly to radiotherapy and fixation alone often fails (progression around the implant), so **resection and endoprosthetic reconstruction** is favoured.
- **Thyroid metastases:** radioiodine-avid lesions may respond to **radioactive iodine**; hypervascular; solitary lesions resected.
- **Prostate:** blastic lesions are painful but fracture less often; respond to androgen deprivation; PSMA-targeted therapy (lutetium-177 PSMA).
- **Breast:** mixed lesions, hormone-responsive; long survival possible, so durable reconstructions are justified.
- **Lung:** shortest survival (often months), fractures rarely heal: simplest effective procedure.
- **Impending fracture versus completed fracture:** **prophylactic fixation** of an impending fracture gives **shorter hospital stay, less blood loss, faster return to walking and better survival** than fixation after the fracture (retrospective data); hence treat impending fractures early.

## 10. Differential diagnosis of a lytic lesion in an older adult (distractors)
| Condition | Clue |
|---|---|
| **Myeloma** | Punched-out lesions, normal ALP, cold bone scan, M-protein, anaemia, renal failure |
| **Primary bone sarcoma** (chondrosarcoma, UPS of bone, osteosarcoma, secondary sarcoma in Paget disease) | Solitary lesion, matrix calcification, periosteal reaction, soft-tissue mass; **biopsy before fixation** |
| **Lymphoma** | Permeative, large soft-tissue mass, well patient |
| **Brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism** | High calcium, high PTH, low phosphate, subperiosteal resorption of phalanges |
| **Paget disease** | Coarse trabeculae, cortical thickening, enlarged bone, raised ALP; **osteoporosis circumscripta** of skull in lytic phase |
| **Osteoporotic insufficiency fracture** | Typical sites (sacrum H-sign, femoral neck), MRI signal pattern |
| **Infection (pyogenic, tuberculosis)** | Disc involvement in spine, fever, raised CRP |
| **Giant cell tumour** | Epiphyseal-metaphyseal, eccentric, skeletally mature (20-40 years) |

> Exam pearl: Breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid cause most bone metastases; spine is the commonest site and proximal femur the commonest long bone. Mirels 9 or more means prophylactic fixation. Fix the whole bone, use cement, replace (do not fix) the femoral neck, give postoperative radiotherapy to the whole implant, and embolise renal and thyroid metastases. For spinal cord compression from a radioresistant solid tumour, decompression with stabilisation plus radiotherapy beats radiotherapy alone (Patchell 2005).
